paragraphs: Learning useful molecular representations by hiding information and reconstructing it becomes complicated when both molecular connectivity and three-dimensional information matter. The decoder needs enough connectivity information to reconstruct hidden atoms, but access to structure can also undermine the intended learning task. 3D-GSRD addresses this tension through selective handling of the encoder’s representations.

Its selective re-mask decoding hides only information relevant to three-dimensional structure while retaining the two-dimensional graph structure. The system combines this mechanism with a 3D Relational-Transformer encoder and a structure-independent decoder. This arrangement preserves useful reconstruction context while, according to the authors’ analysis, strengthening the encoder’s contribution to learning molecular representations.

The reported experiments connect this design to downstream molecular property prediction: 3D-GSRD establishes a new best result on seven of the eight targets in MD17. That finding supports the usefulness of selectively hiding information rather than treating all representation content alike. The contribution is a way to coordinate what the decoder receives with what the encoder is encouraged to learn.
neurips-2025-3d-gsrd-3d-molecular-graph-.tldr: 3D-GSRD selectively re-masks molecular information to improve representation learning, achieving leading results on seven of eight MD17 targets.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces the memory needed to adapt a language model by restricting its updates to a low-rank space. That restriction can also reduce performance relative to updating the full model. Attempts to better approximate full gradients introduce another difficulty: incorporating momentum or adaptive optimization can require intermediate calculations with memory costs approaching full fine-tuning.

AltLoRA uses alternating projections to address the gradient-approximation difficulties associated with jointly updating the low-rank matrices. Its design also incorporates momentum without increasing memory complexity. This targets both the quality of the update and the cost of maintaining its optimization history, rather than improving gradient approximation at the expense of LoRA’s memory advantage.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and theoretical results concerning stable feature learning and robustness to transformation invariance. Across multiple tasks, its experiments show better performance than LoRA and its variants while retaining strong memory efficiency. The stated outcome is a narrower performance gap with full fine-tuning, not an assertion that low-rank adaptation always matches full-model updates.
neurips-2025-altlora-towards-better-grad.tldr: AltLoRA uses alternating projections to improve low-rank adaptation and incorporate momentum while preserving memory efficiency.

paragraphs: Retrieving external information does not ensure that a multimodal language model will use it effectively. The authors identify two obstacles in representative models: attention is unevenly distributed across tokens, and retrieved information can conflict with knowledge stored during training. ALFAR addresses how retrieved knowledge influences an answer after that information is available.

The method makes two adjustments without additional training. First, it moves attention from visual tokens toward relevant context tokens according to how closely the context matches the query. Second, it separates and weights the contributions of stored and contextual knowledge in the output logits, the scores used to choose generated tokens. These adjustments address both information access and competing influences on the response.

Experiments across several models and benchmarks report substantial improvements over leading alternatives. Because ALFAR is designed as a plug-and-play method and requires no additional external tools, its contribution is a way to improve knowledge use within an existing multimodal generation process. The findings support the value of managing attention and knowledge conflicts together.
neurips-2025-boosting-knowledge-utilizat.tldr: ALFAR improves multimodal answers without training by reallocating attention and balancing retrieved knowledge against knowledge stored in the model.

paragraphs: A language-model router chooses which model should answer a query while balancing qualities such as accuracy and cost. A common approach predicts each model’s metrics and then selects a model from those predictions. Errors can accumulate across these stages, and obtaining outcomes from every candidate model for every query is expensive.

This paper instead learns routing decisions from observational records containing only the outcome of the model actually used. Its causal framework directly targets decision regret: the loss associated with a routing choice relative to an optimal choice. For tractable training, the authors introduce a classification-based upper bound and a softmax-weighted approximation. They show that the latter recovers the optimal policy at convergence.

An interval-conditioned architecture extends the approach to differing preferences about cost. Public-benchmark experiments report performance above existing baselines across different embedding models. The contribution combines a decision-focused learning objective with a less exhaustive feedback setting, making the routing problem closer to situations where historical records contain only the model selected at deployment.
neurips-2025-causal-llm-routing-end-to-e.tldr: This causal routing framework learns model-selection policies directly from observational outcomes by optimizing decision regret.

paragraphs: Data can change along several continuous dimensions at once, including time, geography, and socioeconomic conditions. Treating each setting as a separate category, or allowing change along only one axis, misses combinations of these variations. Continuous Domain Generalization asks whether a predictive model can handle unseen domains specified by such combinations.

The paper develops a geometric and algebraic framework in which optimal model parameters across domains lie on a low-dimensional manifold. NeuralLio models transitions between those parameters while enforcing geometric continuity and algebraic consistency. The central idea is to describe how a model should change as the domain changes, using structure shared across the collection of domains.

To accommodate noisy or incomplete descriptions of domain variation, the method includes a gate that suppresses irrelevant dimensions and a strategy based on local charts. Experiments on synthetic data and applications involving remote sensing, scientific documents, and traffic forecasting report improved accuracy and robustness over existing baselines. These findings support modeling multiple continuous sources of variation together.
neurips-2025-continuous-domain-generaliz.tldr: NeuralLio models structured changes in model parameters to generalize across unseen combinations of continuous domain shifts.

paragraphs: EnerVerse connects predictions of a robot’s future surroundings with the actions needed to interact with them. Given instructions, it generates future video in successive chunks using an autoregressive diffusion framework. A sparse context memory supports reasoning over longer periods, while multiple camera views help address ambiguous motion and connect predictions to a three-dimensional world.

The system also includes EnerVerse-D, a data pipeline that combines generative modeling with 4D Gaussian Splatting. The authors use this combination to form a self-reinforcing data loop intended to reduce the gap between simulation and reality. EnerVerse-A then translates the resulting world representations, which include change over time, into physical actions through a policy head.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on their simulation and real-world tasks. For efficient action generation, EnerVerse-A reuses features from the first denoising step and predicts actions in chunks. An eight-step action chunk takes about 280 milliseconds on one RTX 4090. This result ties the representation framework to a concrete execution cost for its action component.
neurips-2025-enerverse-envisioning-embod.tldr: EnerVerse combines multi-view future-video generation, a generative data pipeline, and an action head for robotic manipulation.

paragraphs: Long-horizon robotic planning requires useful short movements to fit together into a coherent longer trajectory. Diffusion planners can struggle when a new task differs from the tasks represented in training. CompDiffuser addresses this problem by learning to compose shorter trajectory chunks from previously seen tasks into solutions for new ones.

The method divides trajectories into overlapping segments and uses one bidirectional diffusion model to learn conditional relationships between them. During generation, information can propagate between segments, allowing neighboring parts to influence each other. The overlap and conditional modeling support physically consistent connections, making the compatibility of the segments part of the generation process itself.

The experiments cover benchmark tasks with differences in environment size, agent state dimension, trajectory type, and training-data quality. Across these evaluations, the authors report substantial improvements over existing methods. The findings support composition as a route to solving tasks beyond the particular complete trajectories seen during training, with the ability to coordinate connections between chunks serving as the central mechanism.
neurips-2025-generative-trajectory-stitc.tldr: CompDiffuser generates plans for new tasks by jointly stitching overlapping trajectory chunks with a bidirectional diffusion model.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can mention an object that is not actually supported by the image it receives. Detecting these object hallucinations requires checking the relationship between generated text and visual evidence. Existing object-level scoring methods often inspect that relationship from either a global or a local perspective, which the authors argue may reduce detection reliability.

GLSim combines both perspectives in a training-free detection framework. It uses embedding similarities between image and text: comparisons between numerical representations of their content. Global and local signals provide complementary evidence about whether an object mention fits the visual input. Combining them lets the detector draw on information at both scales when assessing a possible hallucination.

The authors comprehensively benchmark existing detection methods and report that GLSim outperforms competitive baselines by a substantial margin. The result concerns recognizing unsupported object mentions, rather than establishing that a model will never generate them. Its practical contribution is a detector that improves the use of image-text agreement without requiring an additional training procedure.
neurips-2025-glsim-detecting-object-hall.tldr: GLSim combines global and local image-text similarity to detect object hallucinations without additional training.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution with a more manageable distribution. Mean-field methods gain scalability by assuming independence, but that assumption discards correlations between data instances. The authors identify a gap between methods that model correlations among latent dimensions and methods that capture only simple first-order relationships across instances.

HoT-VI explicitly represents higher-order correlations between instances’ latent variables. It builds the global posterior from overlapping local marginals of dimension k and uses a sequential procedure for efficient parameterized sampling. This provides a way to assemble richer dependencies from smaller distributions while retaining an organized sampling process across the resulting representation.

A conditional correlation parameterization guarantees that the local correlation matrices are positive definite, ensuring their validity. A tree-structured backbone adds flexibility to the dependency patterns the method can express. Experiments on time-series and graph data report better posterior approximations and improved downstream performance when higher-order correlations are modeled. These findings connect a richer dependency structure to benefits in both inference quality and subsequent tasks.
neurips-2025-hot-vi-reparameterizable-va.tldr: HoT-VI models higher-order dependencies between instances using overlapping local distributions and efficient sequential sampling.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network’s structure can be framed as an integer program that searches for a graph with a favorable score. The difficulty is that strong formulations involve exponentially many variables and constraints. Row and column generation avoid introducing everything at once, but deciding which columns to add creates a costly pricing problem.

For likelihood scores with an l0 penalty, the paper reformulates that pricing problem as optimization of a difference of submodular functions. It then applies the Difference of Convex Algorithm as an inexact solver. This focuses the computational improvement on the bottleneck within the larger graph-search procedure, allowing the formulation to grow through dynamically generated rows and columns.

On continuous Gaussian data, the resulting approach produces higher-quality solutions than leading score-based methods, particularly as graphs become denser. It also achieves performance comparable to benchmark constraint-based and hybrid methods as graph size increases. These are empirical findings for the stated data setting; the contribution is a more effective optimization route within score-based structure learning.
neurips-2025-inexact-column-generation-f.tldr: The paper accelerates a bottleneck in Bayesian network structure learning through an inexact difference-of-submodular optimization method.

paragraphs: Adding transformer layers often improves capability, but a formal explanation requires showing that some computations become expressible only at greater depth. This paper establishes such a hierarchy for a specific transformer subclass: models that round to fixed precision everywhere except inside attention. That precision condition defines the scope of the theoretical result.

The proof connects these transformers to the programming language C-RASP through an expressive equivalence that preserves depth. The authors then show that deeper C-RASP programs can express more than shallower ones, transferring that separation back to transformers. Their argument uses an equivalent temporal logic with counting operators, and also establishes a hierarchy for models with positional encodings such as RoPE and ALiBi.

The empirical study asks whether this theory helps predict practical behavior. For transformers without positional encodings, it provides evidence that the theory predicts the depth needed to generalize to longer sequences on a family of dependency tasks. This links a formal expressiveness distinction to observed length generalization in the studied setting.
neurips-2025-knee-deep-in-c-rasp-a-trans.tldr: The paper proves a depth hierarchy for a specified transformer subclass and finds supporting evidence on sequence-length generalization tasks.

paragraphs: A reusable robot skill can have both a discrete identity and continuous settings. Grasping, for example, can be one skill whose arguments specify where to grasp. DEPS learns this kind of structure directly from expert demonstrations, jointly discovering skill policies and a meta-policy that chooses the skill and its parameters at each timestep.

The learning procedure combines temporal variational inference with information-theoretic regularization. These components address degeneracy in latent-variable models, where the learned internal structure can fail to provide useful skills. The intended result is a collection of behaviors that extend over time, have recognizable meaning, and can adapt through their continuous parameters.

Experiments using multitask demonstrations show improved generalization to unseen tasks, with DEPS outperforming multitask and skill-learning baselines on LIBERO and MetaWorld. The authors also demonstrate interpretable learned skills, including grasping with continuous arguments that determine grasp location. Together, the findings connect the learned representation to both task performance and an understandable division between a behavior and its adjustable settings.
neurips-2025-learning-parameterized-skil.tldr: DEPS learns reusable skills with continuous parameters from demonstrations, improving generalization to unseen robotic tasks.

paragraphs: When regulation grants exemptions to open-source AI models, the definition of openness becomes an economic incentive. This paper studies how a regulator’s chosen definition affects two actors: a generalist who creates a general-purpose model and a specialist who adapts that model to a particular task or domain.

The authors build a stylized model of those actors’ strategic responses to regulation. They characterize market equilibria in terms of the generalist’s release decisions and the specialist’s fine-tuning effort. Within this model, they identify an optimal range of openness thresholds that depends on model performance, tying the policy standard to the capabilities of the model being released.

A further result identifies a curve based on initial model performance that distinguishes when changing regulatory penalties or openness thresholds meaningfully changes release strategy. This matters because the two policy instruments need not have the same effect in every modeled setting. The contribution is a theoretical framework for evaluating openness incentives, with conclusions grounded in the strategic relationships of the stylized model.
neurips-2025-modeling-the-economic-impac.tldr: A stylized economic model shows how openness thresholds and regulatory penalties influence model release and downstream fine-tuning incentives.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can generate thousands of tokens before answering, increasing the cost of attending to earlier context and outputs. Sparse attention reduces this pressure, but discarding information can introduce errors that derail reasoning. Multipole Attention addresses the tradeoff by retaining approximate representations of tokens that do not receive exact attention.

The method clusters semantically similar key vectors. Cluster centroids help identify the most important vectors for exact attention and provide approximations for the others. A fast update procedure re-clusters both the input and previously generated tokens, allowing the same approach to support attention over a growing reasoning sequence as generation proceeds.

Evaluations using Qwen-8B and Deepseek-R1-Distil-Qwen2.5-14B show that the method can preserve accuracy on complex reasoning tasks under aggressive attention sparsity. Kernel implementations achieve attention speedups of up to 4.5 times in long-context reasoning applications. That figure applies to attention, while the accuracy results support keeping a coarse representation of less-important context instead of dropping its contribution entirely.
neurips-2025-multipole-attention-for-eff.tldr: Multipole Attention combines exact attention for important tokens with clustered approximations, achieving up to 4.5-fold attention speedups.

paragraphs: This paper studies synthetic faces that look different from a target person yet are recognized as that person by a face-recognition system. It examines an attack setting where repeated, adaptively chosen queries are unavailable. The approach uses structure in the recognition system’s feature space instead of relying on iterative optimization or transfer from a surrogate model.

The authors identify what they call attributed subspheres: regions associated with people sharing an attribute, such as gender or race. Their method uses this structure to generate adversarial faces with few queries. It can also produce faces with high-level attributes chosen by the adversary, extending the objective beyond modifying a particular starting image.

In the reported evaluation against AWS CompareFaces at its default threshold, one non-adaptive query containing 100 face images yields an attack success rate above 93%. The threshold and service are part of that empirical claim. The result demonstrates a vulnerability in the evaluated identity-verification setting even when an attacker cannot repeatedly adjust queries based on feedback.
neurips-2025-non-adaptive-adversarial-fa.tldr: The paper uses face-feature geometry to generate targeted adversarial faces, reporting over 93% success in its non-adaptive AWS evaluation.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based image compression can produce visually convincing reconstructions, but repeated generation steps add decoding latency. OneDC revisits whether those multiple steps are needed for generative compression. It combines a latent compression module with a diffusion generator that reconstructs the image in one step, making semantic guidance especially important to the design.

Instead of relying on text prompts to convey complex visual content, OneDC uses the hyperprior as a semantic signal. A semantic distillation mechanism transfers knowledge from a pretrained generative tokenizer into the hyperprior codec. Training also combines objectives in the pixel and latent domains to improve both faithfulness to the input and perceptual realism.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art perceptual quality with one-step generation, alongside more than 39% bitrate reduction and 20-fold faster decoding compared with prior multi-step diffusion codecs. These findings support the authors’ argument that effective semantic guidance can make a single generation step sufficient for strong compression results in the evaluated setting, substantially reducing the cost of reconstruction.
neurips-2025-one-step-diffusion-based-im.tldr: OneDC uses semantically distilled guidance for one-step image reconstruction, reporting lower bitrates and 20-fold faster decoding than prior multi-step codecs.

paragraphs: Retrieval for an AI answering system has a different goal from retrieval for human browsing: the selected information must help the system reason and respond. Human or synthetic relevance labels provide a fixed training target, which may not adapt well across different retrieval-augmented generation environments. R3 treats retrieval quality as something to improve through interaction with those environments.

The framework trains the retriever with reinforcement learning, allowing it to explore and improve within a given RAG setting. This shifts optimization toward the retriever’s role in the larger answering process. The authors emphasize automating this learning with little manual experimentation or tuning, making adaptation to the surrounding system part of the training approach.

Across diverse tasks, R3 reports a 5.2% improvement over the original retriever and a 4.9% improvement over state-of-the-art retrievers. It also reaches results comparable to LLM-augmented retrieval and RAG systems using post-trained or instruction-tuned language models. The reported training run requires four GPUs and finishes within one day, giving a concrete resource measure for the approach.
neurips-2025-optimizing-retrieval-for-ra.tldr: R3 trains retrievers with reinforcement learning inside RAG environments, improving answering performance with limited manual tuning.

paragraphs: A synthesized program may fit the available examples yet fail on edge cases in the inputs it will actually encounter. This paper introduces transductive program synthesis, which explicitly uses test inputs during synthesis. The goal is to improve robustness when training examples are scarce and the eventual inputs contain cases those examples do not resolve.

The framework treats synthesis as active learning over a finite hypothesis class defined by program outputs. It selects test inputs, asks a language model to predict their outputs, and eliminates hypotheses inconsistent with those predictions. A greedy maximin selection algorithm chooses informative inputs with the aim of reducing the number of language-model queries needed.

Evaluations on Playgol, MBPP+, 1D-ARC, and programmatic world modeling in MiniGrid report significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency. The contribution is a way to use knowledge of the upcoming inputs to focus the synthesis process. Its evidence comes from model-predicted outputs for selected inputs, making targeted information gathering central to narrowing the candidate hypotheses.
neurips-2025-program-synthesis-via-test-.tldr: Transductive program synthesis uses selected test inputs and LLM-predicted outputs to narrow candidate programs more accurately and efficiently.

paragraphs: Clinical reasoning can require medical images, time-series measurements, and written reports together. QoQ-Med introduces open models at 7B and 32B sizes designed to reason across these forms of information. The training approach addresses uneven clinical data distributions, where common domains or easier modalities can dominate learning and leave performance imbalanced.

Domain-aware Relative Policy Optimization adjusts normalized rewards hierarchically according to domain rarity and modality difficulty. The models are trained on 2.61 million instruction-tuning pairs across nine clinical domains. Compared with other critic-free training methods such as GRPO, the authors report an average 43% macro-F1 improvement across the visual domains, tying the reward design to diagnostic performance.

With intensive segmentation training, QoQ-Med can also highlight regions associated with a diagnosis. The reported intersection-over-union is ten times that of open models and reaches OpenAI o4-mini’s performance on this localization measure. The release includes model weights, a modular training pipeline, and intermediate reasoning traces, supporting reproduction and further study of the multimodal training approach.
neurips-2025-qoq-med-building-multimodal.tldr: QoQ-Med uses domain-aware reward scaling to improve clinical reasoning across images, time-series signals, and text reports.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning objectives and constraints often use expected accumulated reward. An average can underrepresent rare but severe outcomes, making it an inadequate description of risk in some high-stakes settings. This paper develops a constrained learning framework that accounts for such distributional concerns using optimized certainty equivalents, or OCEs, as its risk-aware formulation.

The framework provides per-stage robustness properties concerning both reward values and time. It also places the constrained problem within a parameterized strong Lagrangian duality framework. Under appropriate constraint qualifications, this reformulation is exactly equivalent to the original constrained problem. That condition matters: the equivalence is established within the stated mathematical setting rather than asserted for every possible constraint.

The resulting algorithmic recipe can wrap around standard reinforcement-learning solvers, including PPO. The authors establish convergence of their proposed algorithm and use numerical experiments to verify its risk-aware behavior. Together, these results connect a formulation that considers unfavorable outcomes to an implementable learning procedure, while preserving a formal relationship with the original constrained objective.
neurips-2025-risk-averse-constrained-rei.tldr: This framework adds OCE-based risk awareness to constrained reinforcement learning, with conditional duality guarantees and a wrapper for standard solvers.

paragraphs: Generating a sketch from text becomes more useful when users can control its drawing style as well as its subject. This paper presents M3S, a training-free diffusion framework guided by text prompts and reference sketches. It targets a common style-transfer problem: copying unwanted subject matter from the reference along with its visual style.

The method supplies reference features as auxiliary information, using linear smoothing and a style-content guidance mechanism. It avoids overwriting the key and value matrices in self-attention, as previous methods do. The authors report that this design reduces reference-content leakage and improves synthesis, especially when the reference and desired sketch have little structural similarity.

M3S also combines features from multiple reference sketches through a joint AdaIN module, enabling controllable generation with more than one style source. Experiments report high-quality outputs, accurate style alignment, and more flexible control. The contribution is therefore both a way to preserve the intended content during style guidance and a mechanism for coordinating several style references within one generation process.
neurips-2025-text-to-sketch-generation-w.tldr: M3S generates sketches with controllable reference-based styles while reducing unwanted transfer of reference content.

paragraphs: Matrix-vector multiplication can be fast in practice even though worst-case and existing average-case analyses give strong barriers to improvement. This paper investigates whether structure in the matrix explains part of that gap. It studies preprocessing a fixed matrix so that products with subsequently supplied vectors can be answered efficiently.

For an n-by-n Boolean matrix with VC-dimension d, the authors obtain preprocessing time of approximately n squared and query time of approximately n raised to 2 minus 1/d, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The improvement depends on the structural dimension. Since low constant VC-dimensions are observed in much real-world data, the result offers a possible explanation for practical speedups. The authors also extend the approach beyond Boolean matrices using Pollard pseudodimension.

Reductions transfer these gains to dynamic graph problems involving effective resistance, Laplacian solvers, shortest paths, and triangle detection. The paper obtains subquadratic bounds in the high-accuracy regime when the input is structured. These results identify settings where structural restrictions permit efficient algorithms despite conditional lower bounds for more general inputs.
neurips-2025-the-structural-complexity-o.tldr: Low structural dimension enables faster matrix-vector queries and subquadratic algorithms for related dynamic graph problems.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function that explains expert behavior. Alternating adversarial updates to a reward model and a policy can make training unstable. Non-adversarial approaches offer improved stability, but the authors identify a lack of formal guarantees and develop a framework that connects their objectives to a shared mathematical interpretation.

The paper shows that canonical non-adversarial methods explicitly or implicitly maximize the likelihood of expert behavior, equivalently minimizing an expected return gap. From this perspective, it introduces Trust Region Reward Optimization. Using a Minorization-Maximization process, TRRO guarantees monotonic improvement in that likelihood, providing a counterpart in inverse reinforcement learning to TRPO’s stability guarantees in forward learning.

The authors instantiate the framework as Proximal Inverse Reward Optimization, a practical algorithm called PIRO. Experiments on MuJoCo, Gym-Robotics, and a real-world animal-behavior modeling task show results matching or exceeding leading baselines in reward recovery and policy imitation, with high sample efficiency. The theoretical guarantee concerns the TRRO framework, while these experiments demonstrate the practical algorithm’s reported performance.
neurips-2025-trust-region-reward-optimiz.tldr: TRRO guarantees improving expert-behavior likelihood, and its practical PIRO algorithm achieves strong reward recovery and imitation results.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts architectures offer a way to scale transformers through expert components. Most early designs placed those experts in feed-forward layers. Extending the same idea to attention has been harder: existing attention-based expert layers require specialized implementations and, according to the authors, perform less well than their feed-forward counterparts.

UMoE approaches this mismatch by reformulating attention to expose an underlying structure resembling a feed-forward network. That connection provides a common basis for designing expert layers in both parts of the transformer. It also enables parameters to be shared efficiently between attention and feed-forward components, linking two places where earlier designs treated expert computation differently.

The authors report superior performance through UMoE’s attention-based expert layers. The significance of the result is architectural: a different mathematical view of attention makes it possible to unify expert designs and support parameter sharing within the same system. The stated contribution therefore combines improved attention-based MoE performance with a more coordinated use of parameters across transformer components.
neurips-2025-umoe-unifying-attention-and.tldr: UMoE reformulates attention to unify attention and feed-forward expert layers while enabling efficient parameter sharing.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer adapt its behavior using information in the input sequence. Induction heads provide one theoretical account of this ability through their connection to conditional k-gram models. For structured sequences modeled as Markov processes, an open question was whether two layers with one attention head each could represent dependencies of arbitrary order.

The paper proves that this two-layer architecture can represent any conditional k-gram. Earlier known constructions for higher-order sources required at least three layers with one head per layer. The new result therefore sharpens the known relationship between transformer depth and Markov order, establishing that two layers are sufficient for the stated representation task.

The authors also study how their construction can be learned, focusing on a simplified first-order Markov setting. This analysis illustrates how effective in-context representations emerge during training. The distinction between the two results matters: representational sufficiency covers arbitrary order, while the learning-dynamics analysis addresses the simplified first-order case. Together they show substantial capacity in shallow transformers on structured sequence tasks.
neurips-2025-what-one-cannot-two-can-two.tldr: Two transformer layers with one head each suffice to represent any conditional k-gram, sharpening theoretical bounds for structured in-context learning.
